meta.pro_benchmark: A licensed equity pro (Series 7) typically nails Foundations, Greeks, Risk and Pro-Rigor (~90%). Your edge is Flow + Robinhood execution — modules a salaried manager rarely trades. Beat the pro THERE.

questions.question: One standard U.S. equity options contract gives you control over how many shares?
questions.why: One contract = 100 shares. So a quoted premium of $2.00 actually costs you $2.00 × 100 = $200. Forgetting the ×100 is the #1 beginner sizing mistake.
questions.rh_note: On Robinhood a '$2.50' call really debits $250 from your $6k. Always multiply by 100 before you think about size.

questions.question: Buying a CALL gives you the right to do what?
questions.why: A long call = the RIGHT (not obligation) to BUY 100 shares at the strike price up to expiration. You buy calls when you expect the stock to go UP.

questions.question: Buying a PUT gives you the right to do what?
questions.why: A long put = the RIGHT to SELL 100 shares at the strike. Puts gain value when the stock goes DOWN, so they're your bearish bet (or downside insurance).

questions.question: The price you pay to buy an option is called the…
questions.why: Premium is the option's price. As a BUYER you pay premium (it's your max loss). As a SELLER you collect premium (it's your max gain on that leg).

questions.question: The 'strike price' of an option is…
options: The fixed price at which the option can be exercised
questions.why: The strike is the locked-in price you'd buy (call) or sell (put) the 100 shares at if exercised. It never changes for that contract; the stock price moves around it.

questions.question: A CALL is 'in the money' (ITM) when…
options: The stock is below the strike
The stock is above the strike
questions.why: A call is ITM when stock > strike (you could buy cheap and sell at market). A put is ITM when stock < strike. ITM options have real intrinsic value; OTM options are pure hope (time + IV).

questions.question: Intrinsic value of a call equals…
questions.why: Call intrinsic = max(0, spot − strike); it can't go negative. Everything in the premium ABOVE intrinsic is extrinsic (time + implied-vol) value, which decays to zero by expiration.

questions.question: You buy a call. At expiration the stock closes BELOW your strike. What happens?
options: The option expires worthless and you lose the premium
questions.why: An OTM option at expiration is worthless — you lose 100% of the premium paid, no more, no less. This is exactly why far-OTM 'lottery' calls so often go to zero.
questions.rh_note: This is the homelessness trap in miniature: never put money into a long option that you can't afford to lose entirely.

questions.question: What is the maximum a BUYER of a single call or put can lose?
questions.why: A long option's max loss is the premium you paid — that's the whole point of defined risk. Your downside is capped; only SELLERS of naked options face large/unlimited loss.

questions.question: An OTM call has how much intrinsic value?
questions.why: OTM options have zero intrinsic value; 100% of their premium is extrinsic (time + implied volatility). That extrinsic value bleeds away every day (theta) and collapses if IV drops.

questions.question: Delta primarily measures…
options: How much the option price moves per $1 move in the stock
questions.why: Delta = change in option price per $1 move in the underlying. A 0.50 delta call gains ~$0.50/share ($50/contract) if the stock rises $1. Calls have +delta (0→1), puts have −delta (0→−1).

questions.question: Your call has a delta of 0.30. The stock rises $1. Roughly how much does the contract gain (ignoring other greeks)?
questions.why: 0.30 delta × $1 × 100 shares = $30 per contract. Delta is per-share; always ×100 for the contract. Higher-delta (ITM) options track the stock more dollar-for-dollar.

questions.question: Besides price sensitivity, a 0.30 delta is also a rough proxy for…
options: A 30% chance the option finishes in the money
questions.why: Delta loosely approximates the probability of finishing ITM — a 0.30 call has ~30% odds of expiring in the money. That's why low-delta OTM 'lotto' calls usually expire worthless.

questions.question: Theta represents…
options: Time decay — value lost per day
questions.why: Theta is daily time decay. If you're LONG options, theta is negative — every day that passes without movement bleeds premium. Option sellers WANT theta working for them.

questions.question: Theta (time decay) is fastest…
options: In the final ~30 days, especially for at-the-money options
questions.why: Decay accelerates into expiration; the last few weeks erode an ATM option's extrinsic value the fastest. Holding short-dated OTM options overnight with no move is how accounts slowly bleed out.

questions.question: Gamma measures…
options: How fast delta itself changes per $1 move
questions.why: Gamma = the rate of change of delta. It's highest for ATM options near expiration — that's why 0DTE moves so violently: tiny stock moves swing delta (and your P&L) hard in both directions.

questions.question: Vega measures the option's sensitivity to…
questions.why: Vega = price change per 1-point change in implied volatility. Long options have positive vega, so they gain when IV rises and lose when IV falls — the mechanism behind IV crush.

questions.question: 'IV crush' is…
options: A sharp drop in implied volatility (often right after earnings) that deflates premium
questions.why: Before earnings, IV (and premium) is pumped up to price the unknown. Once the news is out, IV collapses — your option can LOSE money even if the stock moves your direction, because vega works against you. This is the classic earnings trap.
questions.rh_note: Buying single calls/puts right before earnings on RH feels exciting and usually loses to IV crush. Beginners get wrecked here constantly.

questions.question: IV Rank / IV Percentile tells you…
options: Where current implied vol sits vs its own past range (is option premium cheap or rich now)
questions.why: IV Rank/Percentile normalizes today's IV against the stock's own history. High IV rank = premium is expensive → favor SELLING premium (spreads/CSPs). Low IV rank = premium cheap → buying long options is less punished by vega.

questions.question: You're bullish but IV is very high (expensive premium). A smarter structure than a naked long call is often…
options: A debit call spread (sell a higher-strike call to offset vega/cost)
questions.why: Buying naked premium into high IV means you're overpaying and exposed to crush. A debit call spread sells some of that rich vega back, lowers your cost and breakeven, and defines risk — at the price of a capped gain.

questions.question: A 'covered call' is…
options: Buying a call with no shares
Owning 100 shares AND selling 1 call against them
questions.why: Covered call = long 100 shares + short 1 call. You collect premium (income) in exchange for capping your upside at the strike. Lower risk than the stock alone — the premium cushions small drops.

questions.question: A 'cash-secured put' (CSP) is…
options: A naked put with no plan
Selling a put while holding enough cash to buy 100 shares if assigned
questions.why: CSP = short put fully backed by cash to buy the shares at the strike. You get PAID to potentially buy a stock you already like at a lower price. If it's not assigned, you keep the premium as income.
questions.rh_note: On $6k you can only secure a put where 100 shares (strike × 100) fits your buying power — e.g. a $15 strike needs $1,500 set aside.

questions.question: 'The wheel' strategy is…
options: Sell CSP → if assigned, own shares → sell covered calls → repeat
questions.why: The wheel cycles premium income: sell cash-secured puts to get paid (and maybe buy shares cheap), then sell covered calls on those shares to get paid again, repeating. A staple for steady, lower-variance income on stocks you'd be happy to own.

questions.question: A debit (vertical) call spread is…
options: Buying a call and selling a higher-strike call, same expiration
Buying a call and a put
questions.why: Buy a lower-strike call, sell a higher-strike call (same expiry). It's cheaper than the naked call, lowers your breakeven, and defines max loss = net debit — but caps your max gain at the spread width.

questions.question: Which of these has UNDEFINED (potentially huge) risk?
questions.why: A naked short call has theoretically unlimited loss — a stock can rise forever. Long calls, spreads, and CSPs all have defined or bounded risk. This is why brokers gate naked calls behind the highest approval level.

questions.question: You're moderately bullish and want to cut both cost and IV exposure. Best fit?
questions.why: A debit call spread gives you defined-risk bullish exposure at a fraction of the naked-call cost and trims vega. You give up unlimited upside (capped at the short strike) in exchange for a cheaper, higher-probability position.

questions.question: You want to get PAID while waiting to buy a stock you like at a lower price. Use a…
questions.why: Selling a cash-secured put pays you premium now; if the stock dips to your strike you buy it (at an effective discount = strike − premium), and if it doesn't, you simply keep the cash. Ideal income tool on names you'd own anyway.

questions.question: A bull PUT spread (credit spread) makes money when…
options: The stock stays above your short strike, so you keep the net credit
questions.why: Sell a higher-strike put, buy a lower-strike put for protection. You collect a credit and profit if the stock stays ABOVE the short strike at expiration. Defined risk = strike width − credit. A high-probability, theta-positive way to be mildly bullish.

questions.question: On a small $6k account, the SAFEST way to earn income on a stock you'd happily own is usually…
options: A defined-risk credit spread or a cash-secured put you can actually afford
questions.why: Defined-risk credit spreads and affordable CSPs cap your downside and pay you premium — exactly what a small account needs. Naked calls (unlimited risk) and 0DTE scalps (high variance) are account-killers on $6k.

questions.question: A long straddle (buy a call AND a put at the same strike) profits when…
options: The stock makes a BIG move either direction (more than the combined premium)
questions.why: A straddle is a bet on volatility/magnitude, not direction — you need a move bigger than both premiums combined to profit. Its enemies are theta and IV crush, so it's a poor 'hold through earnings' play despite feeling clever.

questions.question: On a $6k account, roughly how much should ONE trade be allowed to lose at most (Mike's discipline)?
questions.why: Sizing every trade as a small fraction of current equity (a hard cap around $100–250 on $6k) means no single loss can cripple you. Survival first — you can't compound an account you blew up.
questions.rh_note: This is the core anti-homelessness rule: cap each trade's max loss, then you can be wrong many times and still be in the game.

questions.question: Putting $1,500 of a $6k account into a single same-day (0DTE) call is…
options: Wildly over-sized — 25% of the account at near-total-loss risk
questions.why: That's 25% of your account on a position that can easily go to zero by the close. A couple of those wipes you out. Position size, not conviction, is what keeps you solvent.

questions.question: The maximum you can lose on a long option position is…
questions.why: Long options can lose 100% of premium and no more — so your position size literally equals 'money I'm willing to lose entirely.' Size each long-option trade as if it could go to zero, because it can.

questions.question: Risking exactly 2% of a $6,000 account on a trade means a max loss of…
questions.why: 2% × $6,000 = $120. Defining your dollar risk FIRST (then choosing a contract/size that fits it) is how pros size. Most blow-ups come from sizing by excitement instead of by a fixed risk budget.

questions.question: 'Assignment risk' on a short option means…
options: You may be obligated to buy (short put) or deliver (short call) 100 shares
questions.why: If you SELL an option and it's ITM, the buyer can exercise — you must buy 100 shares (short put) or sell/deliver 100 shares (short call). That's why CSPs need the cash and covered calls need the shares; uncovered, it can force a position you can't afford.

questions.question: Time decay (theta) hurts you MOST when you…
options: Hold long options that aren't moving, especially short-dated ones
questions.why: Long options bleed theta daily; the closer to expiration and the more OTM, the faster the bleed. If your thesis needs 'a move soon' and the stock chops sideways, theta quietly eats the position.

questions.question: When a trade's thesis is clearly invalidated, the disciplined move is to…
options: Cut the loss and protect capital
Hold to expiration no matter what
questions.why: Capital preservation beats hope. Exiting a broken thesis keeps a small loss small; averaging down on a losing OPTION (with theta/IV decay) usually compounds the damage. Live to trade tomorrow.

questions.question: Why do brokers like Robinhood block naked (uncovered) calls for most retail accounts?
options: Unlimited loss potential — a stock can rise without bound
questions.why: A naked short call's loss is theoretically unlimited (no ceiling on a stock price), so it requires the highest options approval and serious margin. Retail tiers are restricted to defined-risk structures to stop catastrophic blow-ups.

questions.question: Spreading $6k thinly across ten tiny far-OTM 'lottery' calls vs sizing fewer defined-risk trades — the lottery approach mainly…
options: Maximizes theta/IV bleed and usually drips the account to zero
questions.why: Many cheap far-OTM calls each have low probability and high theta/IV decay — collectively they tend to bleed out. Concentrating on fewer, higher-probability, defined-risk setups (sized to a fixed risk budget) is far more survivable.

questions.question: The single habit that most protects a small options account from ruin is…
options: Strict position sizing / defined risk on every trade
questions.why: You will be wrong often — everyone is. Consistent small position sizing and defined risk mean being wrong costs you a survivable amount each time. That, not prediction, is what keeps you in the game long enough to win.

questions.question: '0DTE' refers to an option that…
questions.why: 0DTE = zero days to expiration (expires today). It's almost all gamma and theta: tiny stock moves swing it hard, and what's OTM at the close goes to zero. Thrilling, very high variance, easy to blow up on.

questions.question: For a directional SWING trade, a common DTE 'sweet spot' that balances cost and theta is…
questions.why: ~30–45 DTE gives your thesis time to play out without paying for excessive premium, and theta decay is still moderate (it accelerates hardest inside the final couple weeks). Buys you room to be right without bleeding out fast.

questions.question: Compared with an OTM call (delta ~0.30), an ITM call (delta ~0.70) generally…
options: Costs more but tracks the stock more 1-for-1, with less theta/IV risk and higher win probability
questions.why: Higher-delta ITM calls have intrinsic value, move closer to dollar-for-dollar with the stock, carry less extrinsic (so less theta/IV bleed), and have higher odds of finishing ITM. You pay more up front and get less raw leverage, but fewer ways to lose to time and vol.

questions.question: If you want the HIGHEST probability of profit and the LEAST theta/IV risk on a directional bet, lean toward…
options: Slightly ITM, a bit more time
questions.why: Slightly-ITM with a little more DTE maximizes the share of intrinsic value (real, non-decaying) and minimizes the share you can lose to theta and IV crush. It's the 'I want to be right and survive being early' choice.

questions.question: Buying single options right BEFORE an earnings release mainly exposes you to…
questions.why: Pre-earnings IV is inflated; after the report IV collapses and premium deflates. You can be right on direction and still lose because vega worked against you. If you must play earnings, defined-risk spreads blunt the crush better than naked long options.

questions.question: A sound profit-taking rule for LONG premium (bought calls/puts) is to…
options: Take profits at a preset target (e.g. +50–100%) rather than squeezing the last dollar
questions.why: Theta and reversals erode unrealized gains fast. Booking profits at a planned target (and cutting losers at a planned stop) turns paper gains into real ones and removes emotion. 'Letting it ride' on a long option often gives it all back.

questions.question: Holding a still-OTM option into its final week to expiration exposes you mostly to…
options: Rapid theta decay — it needs the move NOW or it's worth ~0
questions.why: In the last week, an OTM option's extrinsic value evaporates quickly; without an immediate move it heads to zero. If you're not in profit and the catalyst hasn't hit, that final week is where most of the loss happens.

questions.question: The stock has ALREADY made most of its expected catalyst move. Buying short-dated OTM calls to chase is…
options: Late and low-EV — the move is largely priced in and theta/IV now fight you
questions.why: Chasing after the spike means you buy inflated premium (IV often pumped) right as the easy move is done. You're now paying for a move that's mostly happened, with theta and a likely IV fade working against you. Best entries are BEFORE the crowd, not after.

questions.question: To stay directional while CUTTING theta and IV-crush risk, you'd generally…
options: Go slightly ITM and a bit longer-dated
questions.why: More intrinsic value (ITM) + more time (longer DTE) shrinks the fraction of your premium that's exposed to time decay and vega. You trade some leverage and cost for a far more forgiving, survivable directional position.

questions.question: A reasonable hard stop discipline on a bought option is to…
options: Predefine a max loss (e.g. −50% of premium or thesis-break) and exit when hit
questions.why: Deciding your exit BEFORE you enter removes the in-the-moment emotion that turns a small loss into a big one. A predefined stop (a % of premium or 'the thesis broke') keeps each loss inside your risk budget.

questions.question: An options 'sweep' is…
options: An aggressive order split across multiple exchanges to fill immediately — signals urgency
questions.why: A sweep takes whatever liquidity is available across exchanges to get filled fast, paying up for immediacy. That urgency is why sweeps are watched as potential 'smart money in a hurry' — though they can still be hedges.

questions.question: A 'block' trade is…
options: A single large, often privately negotiated order — sizeable but usually less urgent than a sweep
questions.why: Blocks are big single prints, frequently institutional and negotiated. They show conviction by SIZE, but unlike sweeps they aren't screaming 'fill me now.' Reading WHICH kind it is helps you judge urgency.

questions.question: An options trade printing AT or ABOVE the ask ('ask-side') generally suggests…
options: A buyer-initiated, aggressive order (bullish if it's calls)
questions.why: Paying the ask = the buyer wanted in badly enough to cross the spread, i.e. buyer-initiated aggression. Ask-side CALL buying leans bullish; bid-side selling leans the other way. (Always check it's an opening trade, not a hedge.)

questions.question: A 'golden sweep' on a flow scanner usually flags…
options: An unusually large (often repeated) sweep tagged as high-conviction
questions.why: Golden sweeps are the biggest, most aggressive sweeps — a high-premium urgent bet worth a closer look. High conviction by the prints' size/urgency, but 'high conviction' is not 'guaranteed' — it's a lead, not a signal to copy blindly.

questions.question: Open interest (OI) vs volume: which statement is right?
options: OI = total contracts outstanding; volume = contracts traded today. Volume >> OI hints at NEW positioning
questions.why: Volume is today's activity; OI is the running total of open contracts. When today's volume dwarfs the existing OI at a strike, it signals fresh positioning rather than traders closing — a stronger 'something's happening here' tell.

questions.question: Why might huge institutional CALL buying NOT actually be a bullish signal to copy?
options: It could be a hedge (e.g. against a short stock position) or one leg of a spread — premium size alone doesn't reveal direction
questions.why: A big call print can be a hedge, a spread leg, or a roll — not a naked directional bet. Without seeing the full structure (and the stock position behind it), 'big call buy = bullish' is a trap. Context and trade structure matter more than raw premium.

questions.question: You see a credible BULLISH flow alert. On a $6k account, the sensible way to follow it is…
options: Buy the exact same far-OTM lotto contract they did
Take a smaller, defined-risk position — often slightly ITM or a spread, matching or shortening their DTE
questions.why: Institutions have size, hedges, and time you don't. Translate the idea into YOUR account: a smaller, higher-probability, defined-risk expression (slightly ITM or a spread), sized to your risk cap. Copying their exact cheap far-OTM strike usually just donates theta.
questions.rh_note: This is your real edge over a salaried equity manager: you can act on retail flow nimbly. Just size it to $100–250 risk and pick a strike that can actually survive being early.

questions.question: Repeated/persistent flow on the SAME strike across several days suggests…
options: Sustained conviction / accumulation — a stronger tell than a one-off print
questions.why: A single print can be noise or a hedge; the same strike lighting up day after day points to ongoing accumulation or conviction. Persistence is one of the better filters for separating real positioning from one-off prints.

questions.question: The most common mistake retail makes when copying 'unusual options activity' is…
options: Buying cheap far-OTM short-dated calls (lottery tickets) that bleed theta and usually expire worthless
questions.why: Retail sees a big bullish print and grabs the cheapest far-OTM weekly to 'leverage' it — exactly the contract with the worst probability and the fastest theta/IV bleed. The pros' edge isn't the strike; it's size, structure, hedging and timing you can't replicate by buying lotto tickets.

questions.question: When deciding ITM vs OTM off a strong bullish flow signal, choosing more ITM (higher delta) mainly buys you…
options: Higher probability and tighter tracking of the stock, at a higher cost and less raw leverage
questions.why: If the flow has real conviction and you want to be PAID for being right (not just gamble on a perfect strike), ITM gives higher odds and less time/vol risk. OTM only wins if the move is big and fast — great when right, but most of the time the ITM choice is the survivable one.

questions.question: The Pattern Day Trader (PDT) rule means an account UNDER $25k equity is limited to…
options: About 3 day trades per rolling 5 business days (a 4th flags PDT)
questions.why: Under $25k, more than 3 day trades (open+close same day) in 5 business days triggers a PDT flag and restrictions. On a $6k account this caps how aggressively you can scalp 0DTE — plan swing trades that don't burn day-trade counts.
questions.rh_note: RH enforces PDT. Getting flagged can freeze your day-trading for 90 days — a real constraint on a $6k account.

questions.question: Your long call is ITM at expiration but you can't afford to exercise (buy 100 shares). On Robinhood, what typically happens?
options: RH will generally try to SELL the ITM option for you before close to avoid an exercise you can't cover
You're forced into margin debt automatically with no warning
questions.why: ITM options are auto-exercised by the OCC at expiration if left open. Because exercise needs capital you may not have, RH usually auto-SELLS your ITM long option near the close instead. Don't rely on it though — close ITM options yourself before expiration to stay in control.

questions.question: Robinhood's basic options level lets you…
options: Buy calls/puts and run covered positions — but NOT naked calls
questions.why: Retail tiers allow long calls/puts, covered calls, and cash-secured puts, but uncovered (naked) calls are restricted because of their unlimited risk. Knowing what your approval level permits stops you from planning trades the platform won't let you place.

questions.question: To sell a cash-secured put on Robinhood you need…
options: Enough cash/buying power to buy 100 shares at the strike if assigned
questions.why: 'Cash-secured' literally means RH sets aside strike × 100 in buying power to cover potential assignment. A $20 strike put ties up $2,000. On $6k that limits you to lower-priced underlyings — plan around your actual buying power.

questions.question: A call quoted at $3.00 on Robinhood will debit your account…
questions.why: $3.00 premium × 100 shares = $300. Robinhood shows the per-share premium; the contract costs 100×. On a $6k account that single contract is already 5% of your capital at risk — size accordingly.

questions.question: 'Early assignment' on a short equity option can happen…
options: Any time before expiration — equity options are American-style (notably around ex-dividend for short calls, or when deep ITM)
questions.why: U.S. equity options are American-style, so a short option can be assigned ANY day it's ITM — especially short calls right before an ex-dividend date, or deep-ITM options. If you sell options, early assignment is a real risk you must be able to cover.

questions.question: If you sold an option and can't afford to be assigned 100 shares, the right move before expiration is to…
options: Buy the option back (close it) before it's assigned
Let it assign and sort it out later
questions.why: Closing (buying back) a short option removes the assignment obligation entirely. Waiting and hoping risks being forced into a 100-share position your $6k can't cover, possibly triggering a margin call or forced liquidation.

questions.question: Aggressively day-trading options on a $6k Robinhood account risks TWO account-killers at once:
options: Hitting the PDT day-trade limit AND blowing up through oversizing
questions.why: Frequent same-day options trades both burn your limited PDT day-trade count (under $25k) and tempt oversized, high-variance bets. Either can end the account — together they're why disciplined swing/defined-risk trading suits a small account far better.

questions.question: Breakeven at expiration for a LONG CALL is…
questions.why: A long call only nets a profit once the stock clears strike + premium. Example: $50 strike, $2 premium → breakeven $52. Knowing breakeven before you enter tells you how big a move you actually need.

questions.question: Breakeven at expiration for a LONG PUT is…
questions.why: A long put profits below strike − premium. Example: $50 strike, $2 premium → breakeven $48; the stock must fall past $48 for you to net a gain. Mirror image of the call breakeven.

questions.question: Maximum loss on a NAKED (uncovered) short put is…
options: Roughly (strike − premium) × 100, if the stock goes to zero
questions.why: A short put's worst case is the stock falling to $0: you're obligated to buy at the strike, losing (strike − premium) per share × 100. Large but finite (unlike a naked call's unlimited risk). This is the real exposure behind 'getting paid to buy.'

questions.question: On a DEBIT call spread, maximum gain equals…
options: The premium of the long leg
questions.why: Max gain = the distance between strikes minus what you paid, ×100; max loss = the net debit. Example: buy 50 / sell 55 for $2 → max gain (5 − 2)×100 = $300, max loss $200. Defined on both ends — that's the appeal.

questions.question: Put-call parity describes the fixed relationship between…
options: A call, a put, the stock, and the strike (C − P = S − PV(K))
questions.why: Put-call parity (C − P = S − present value of strike) ties same-strike/expiry calls, puts and the stock together; arbitrage keeps them aligned. It's the backbone fact behind synthetic positions and why mispriced legs get arbed away fast.

questions.question: An option's total premium is always made of…
questions.why: Premium = intrinsic (real, exercise value) + extrinsic (time + implied-volatility value). At expiration extrinsic = 0, so only intrinsic remains. Understanding the split tells you how much of your price is 'real' vs 'decaying.'

questions.question: U.S. single-stock equity options are generally ___-style, while many broad index options are ___-style.
questions.why: Equity options are American (exercisable any time before expiry → early-assignment risk). Many index options (e.g. SPX) are European (exercise only at expiration, cash-settled). The style changes your assignment and settlement risk.

questions.question: Maximum gain on a covered call (long 100 shares + short 1 call) is…
options: (Strike − stock cost + premium) × 100 — upside capped above the strike
questions.why: Selling the call caps your upside: best case the stock finishes at/above the strike and you make (strike − your cost + premium) ×100. You trade unlimited upside for premium income and a small downside cushion — the classic income tradeoff.

questions.question: On a covered call, your downside breakeven on the shares is…
questions.why: The premium you collected lowers your effective cost: breakeven = what you paid for the shares minus the call premium. Below that you're net losing on the position — the premium only cushions a limited drop, it doesn't fully protect you.

questions.question: Maximum gain on a long call vs maximum loss on a long call:
options: Max gain theoretically unlimited; max loss = premium paid
Max gain = strike; max loss = unlimited
questions.why: A long call's upside is theoretically unlimited (no ceiling on the stock) while its downside is capped at the premium. That asymmetric payoff — small defined risk, large potential reward — is the core reason traders buy calls.
